analysis.one_liner: Extends unpaid family and medical leave to part-time and newer workers and bars paying part-timers less for equal work.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 17, 2025 with 8 Democratic and independent Senate sponsors and referred to the HELP Committee; no hearing, vote, or further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change two sets of rules that apply to people working part-time or short stints. First, it would make employees eligible for unpaid, job-protected family and medical leave after 90 days on the job, instead of the current rules that require 12 months of service and 1,250 hours worked in the prior year [S2]. Second, it would make it unlawful for an employer to pay part-time or temporary workers less than full-time workers doing the same job, to give them worse scheduling notice or fewer benefits, or to hire outside workers while existing employees are asking for more hours — with damages, back pay, and Attorney's fees for workers who sue [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Part-time, temporary, and new employees — concentrated in retail, restaurants, warehouses, and care work, and disproportionately women — gain leave eligibility after 90 days, equal pay for equal work, better scheduling notice, and first shot at extra hours. Workers at franchised businesses are covered because the bill counts employees across a franchise system together.

how_it_helps.text: Employees would qualify for unpaid, job-protected family and medical leave after 90 days of employment, replacing the current 12-month and 1,250-hour requirements; the same change applies to congressional staff, federal employees, and DC and presidential appointees [S2].

The bill also removes the exclusion that lets employers deny leave to their 10% highest-paid salaried employees, and strikes the 26-week cap on leave to care for a seriously injured service member [S2].

Employers with more than 15 employees — counting part-timers and temp workers, and counting employees across an integrated enterprise, chain of businesses, or franchise network in the aggregate — could not pay or treat workers worse for working fewer hours or shorter stints when the jobs require substantially equal skill, effort, and responsibility [S2].

Differential treatment on pay, scheduling notice and input, pro-rata benefits accrual, and promotion opportunities is expressly listed as discrimination; employers would have to document, at hiring, each employee's desired weekly hours and availability, and offer existing employees those hours before hiring new staff, contractors, or staffing agencies, paying existing employees for any covered hour a new hire works instead [S2].

Workers could sue in federal or state court, individually or as a group, for lost wages and benefits, interest, an equal amount in liquidated damages, reinstatement or promotion, and attorney's fees; the Labor Department could investigate, subpoena records, and seek civil penalties of $500 to $5,000 per violation for willful and repeated violations, adjusted for inflation [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with sizable part-time or temporary workforces — retail, restaurant, warehouse, franchise, and staffing companies above the 15-employee threshold — bear higher wage and benefit costs for part-time staff, scheduling and record-keeping obligations (records kept at least 3 years), exposure to double-damage lawsuits, and a rule against hiring outside help while existing employees want the hours.

drawbacks.text: The employer threshold is just 15 employees, counted across an entire franchise network or integrated enterprise, which is far lower than the 50-employee threshold in current FMLA law — small franchisees and small firms would face equal-pay, scheduling, and damages obligations that many federal employment laws exempt them from [S2].

The offer-of-work rule requires paying existing employees for hours a new hire or contractor works instead of them, even when the employee was not actually scheduled or working — a compensation obligation that goes beyond wage payment for work performed and could be costly in industries with fluctuating demand [S2].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the compliance burden: employers must collect and update written availability statements from every worker and keep compliance records for at least 3 years, and the 'substantially equal skill, effort, and responsibility' standard invites litigation over borderline cases, such as whether a part-timer and full-timer in related roles have comparable jobs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gains are concrete: leave after 90 days instead of after a year of full-time hours, equal pay for equal work, and a right to the extra hours they ask for before new hires get them. The costs fall on employers and, to the extent they raise prices or trim headcount to offset them, partly on consumers — and the 15-employee, franchise-aggregated threshold plus pay-for-unscheduled-hours rule make this a broad and demanding bill by the standards of federal wage law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 17, 2025 and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, which has taken no action on it yet.

narrative.text: Senator Warren introduced the Part-Time Worker Bill of Rights Act in the Senate on December 17, 2025, joined by seven cosponsors (Booker, Markey, Padilla, Whitehouse, Sanders, Murray, and Baldwin) [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it remains [S4].
The Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill could still receive a hearing, markup, or floor vote, but none has been scheduled [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. Because the bill has not advanced, part-time workers have not gained the protections, and employers have not taken on the new obligations; the outcome so far favors whichever side prefers the status quo for another session, since most bills referred to committee without a hearing never advance in a two-year Congress — a general pattern, not something specific to this bill's sources [S4].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No winner yet; bill sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited seven Senate cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: Sens. Booker, Markey, Padilla, Whitehouse, Sanders, Murray, and Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction; all seven are Democrats or independents allied with Democrats, with no Republican support.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors are Democrats or independents; the cosponsor list shows 6 Democrats and 1 independent and no Republicans, and no member has acted in opposition yet because the bill has not moved past introduction.

industries.industry: Retail, restaurant, warehouse, and franchise employers with large part-time workforces
industries.note: These employers would have to pay part-timers the same as comparable full-timers, give them pro-rata benefits and scheduling input, offer existing employees hours before hiring outside help, and keep 3 years of compliance records. The industry's cost here is the worker's wage and benefit gain, so its interest runs against the public's in this bill.

Employers could not bring in staffing-agency or contract workers to fill hours that existing employees have asked for, cutting off a key sales channel. The restriction protects workers' access to hours, so the agency's interest runs against the public's.

The bill counts employees across an entire franchise network in the aggregate, so small franchisees under a large brand would be covered once the network passes 15 employees. It also targets 'any person acting in the interest of an employer,' reaching franchisors.

industries.industry: Hospitality, care, and other sectors that use part-time and short-duration scheduling as a cost strategy
industries.note: The bill would not ban part-time work, but paying part-timers equally, granting them benefits, and compensating them for offered-but-unscheduled hours removes much of the cost advantage of keeping workers under 40 hours and under a year of tenure.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in the HELP Committee since introduction with no hearing or markup scheduled and no Republican support. In a Senate where most bills die in committee, a labor bill introduced late in the first session with one-party sponsorship is unlikely to advance on its own; its realistic path is as a vehicle for amendments, a talking point in a Democratic platform, or a reintroduction in the next Congress.
